transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-03
Start: 16:30 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Huang (Redwood SRE), Alex Rivera (Sentinel Infra Lead), Dana Kim (Sentinel ML Eng), Priya Sinha (Sentinel Security)

AutoSummary (auto-generated, optional): quick rpm - wide ranging, some audio dropouts, vals..

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to kick off with an overview of what you said in the intake form — you're most interested in reducing per-token cost on MoE models while keeping p90 latency under 250ms, is that right?

[00:18] Alex Rivera: Yeah that's right. We're evaluating a mix of things — mostly Mistral and Qwen for standard tasks, and a MoE mix for some high-throughput routing experiments. Latency matters for UI, but some batch jobs can piggyback.

[00:36] Priya Patel: Quick clarification, when you say MoE mix, are you running a custom gating layer or using off-the-shelf MoE like fairseq/flash?

[00:44] Dana Kim: We're prototyping with a community MoE gate right now—it's pretty rough. The gating is top-k with a capacity factor tuned to 1.5 but we haven't simulated the real routing costs across our long-tail prompts.

[01:03] Marcus Huang: (background) Also, curious about your infra — on-prem versus VPC? That will change where we can do certain kernel optimizations and KMS calls.

[01:12] Alex Rivera: We'll probably do a hybrid. Sensitive models run in our VPC private deployment; non-sensitive inference can go to hosted. But the latency SLA forces most user-facing traffic to be local.

[01:28] Jordan Lee: Great. Today we'll walk through three areas: 1) modeling MoE routing cost and recommended gating strategies, 2) RoPE/positional scaling for long sequences (we've seen mis-calibration when you scale sequence length), and 3) practical runtime knobs — KV cache sizing, continuous batching, and quantization tradeoffs. Sound good?

[01:46] Alex Rivera: Yep. Also want to touch on SSO/KMS integration and audit logs — Priya Sinha will chime in later.

[02:00] Priya Patel: I'll start with MoE routing. High level: the gating step itself is cheap, but every router decision that sends a token to multiple experts multiplies memory + compute. So the big levers are: top-1 vs top-2 routing, capacity factor, and expert balancing. For cost, top-1 with balanced experts often wins, but accuracy can drop for some tasks.

[02:26] Dana Kim: We saw a 30% quality gain moving from top-1 to top-2 on long-context summarization, but cost went up ~60% in our naive plumbing.

[02:37] Priya Patel: That's very typical. Two practical strategies: 1) soft-routing hybrid — use top-1 at inference, but selectively top-2 for prompts flagged by a cheap classifier, 2) probabilistic gating where you only route to top-2 for tokens with gating entropy above a threshold. Both reduce avg routing cost while preserving tail quality.

[02:59] Jordan Lee: We usually recommend a cheap pre-router classifier — like a distilled binary that says "this request needs high-diversity routing". It reduces the number of tokens hitting multi-expert paths.

[03:15] Alex Rivera: How do you quantify the routing cost? Is it strictly extra FLOPs or also memory movement and kernel fusion penalties on GPU?

[03:25] Priya Patel: It's all of the above. On modern GPUs the memory-bound cost of scattering tokens to expert memory and reassembling them can be the dominant factor. We measure in three axes: extra tokens processed (tokens * expert_count), peak activation memory delta, and additional kernel launches. We provided a simple spreadsheet in the deck — but Priya admits the spreadsheet has assumptions that can be off by 20% per-hardware.

[03:53] Dana Kim: Any suggestions on kernel-level ops? We use an open runtime that doesn't fuse the scatter/gather so we lose a lot.

[04:03] Marcus Huang: In Redwood's runtime we try to fuse gating+scatter for common MoE patterns and keep expert tensors in GPU-local pinned buffers to avoid cross-device copies, that reduces the wall clock by about 25-35% in our internal runs. But it's hardware dependent.

[04:23] Jordan Lee: Next up RoPE. We've had customers who extend sequence lengths (e.g., 8k to 32k) and noticed drift — perplexing outputs and lower likelihoods. Short version: RoPE positional embeddings don't always scale linearly; you need to adjust the base frequency (theta) and possibly rescale attention bias.

[04:46] Alex Rivera: Can you expand on "rescale"? We simply zero-pad past trained length—terrible idea?

[04:54] Priya Patel: Zero padding mostly works for generative few-shot with short prompts, but for long retrieval contexts you get aliasing. Two approaches: 1) linear RoPE rescaling where you apply a multiplicative factor to angles beyond the trained max, 2) rotary interpolation where you remap positions via a learned or heuristic interpolation. Both are heuristic and require evals. We suggest running small cal tests: holdout evaluation set using your real sessions.

[05:22] Dana Kim: Is there a recommended default factor? We tried doubling base freq and got mixed results.

[05:28] Priya Patel: Defaults vary by model family. For Llama variants keep theta multiplier near 1.0–1.2; Mistral tends to be more sensitive, Qwen is weird because it mixes absolute-like encodings. The safe path is to sweep small multipliers and monitor perplexity and downstream metric.

[05:46] Jordan Lee: Also watch kv-cache eviction policies. If you extend sequence length, your KV cache memory grows linearly with context. We recommend prefix summarization or adaptive eviction when 2/3 of memory budget is used.

[06:02] Alex Rivera: For prefix summarization, do you mean canonical summaries piped back to the prompt or truncated KV entries?

[06:10] Priya Patel: Both patterns exist. Summarization reduces token count and can keep semantics; truncated KVs are cheaper but can lose fine-grain context. Another hybrid — keep dense KVs for recent tokens and compressed/hashed KVs for older tokens. We've seen 20–40% memory wins with minimal quality loss.

[06:28] Dana Kim: Our biggest worry is latency spikes when the cache warms or when a routing spike causes many experts to fire. How does Redwood handle SLO isolation?

[06:38] Marcus Huang: We do a few things: 1) request-level SLO routing — hot requests can be served on a low-latency node pool that is narrowly provisioned (higher cost), 2) automated fallback to a quantized or smaller dense model when percentile latency rises, and 3) opportunistic token shedding — drop expensive reranking or non-critical tokens from pipeline. The fallback policy is configurable per-customer.

[07:05] Alex Rivera: Fallback to quantized — we worry about quality regressions. Any specific quantization recipes you recommend?

[07:13] Priya Patel: For Llama-family, 4-bit GPTQ works well if you calibrate with your data distribution. Mistral often tolerates symmetric 8-bit more gracefully. Qwen's weight layout sometimes favors mixed-precision kernels. The big warning: don't quantize adapters or small dense heads aggressively — they can be brittle. Also watch out for KV cache format compatibility when mixing quantized kernels.

[07:41] Dana Kim: How do you test quantization quality quickly? Full evals are expensive.

[07:47] Priya Patel: We recommend a 3-stage approach: 1) small eval set (1–2k examples) for quick signal, 2) synthetic adversarial prompts that stress hallucination and safety, 3) production shadow tests for a week capturing p95/perp deltas. The small eval should give early pass/fail.

[08:08] Jordan Lee: Let's talk batching. Continuous batching vs fixed micro-batch windows — tradeoffs?

[08:15] Priya Patel: Continuous batching lumps requests opportunistically into larger GPU batches with a tight latency cap. If your distribution has many sub-100ms prep times, continuous batching reduces tokens/sec cost. But it adds jitter to p50. Fixed windows give more predictable latency but often lower utilization. For Sentinel's UI use-case, we suggest a hybrid: default continuous batching with a max-delay cap of ~25ms for interactive routes.

[08:42] Alex Rivera: What about tail latency when a giant batch triggers an OOM?

[08:48] Marcus Huang: We do adaptive batch shaping that inspects incoming seq lengths and avoids combining a 20k-token request with many 1-token requests. We also pre-reserve headroom in the allocator for worst-case expert fan-out in MoEs.

[09:02] Dana Kim: VPC stuff — latency of KMS calls when decrypting model keys on boot. We have strict policies that HSM calls must be inside our net, with mTLS. Any gotchas?

[09:13] Jordan Lee: For Private deployment we provide a local KMS plugin option so keys never leave your VPC, and we support HSM integrations. The main gotcha is startup latency for decrypting large model shards — we recommend key caching and not decrypting on every shard load. Also watch network policy for NFS/GPUDirect traffic.

[09:34] Priya Sinha: Regarding audit logs and compliance, do you persist raw user inputs in hosted mode? We need to know retention and redaction behaviors.

[09:42] Jordan Lee: Hosted mode can be configured to not persist raw inputs; we provide token-level cost and latency metrics, and audit logs that track request IDs without storing plaintext by default. For Enterprise we sign a retention policy in the contract. We'll send the security pack with exact fields.

[09:59] Alex Rivera: Small question on RoPE again — you said interpolation — can you give a concrete example or pointer?

[10:06] Priya Patel: Sure; think of remapping position p to p' = floor(p * scale) + frac interpolation between neighboring rotary bases. It's slightly messy, often implemented as a small preprocessing kernel before attention. We'll drop a link to a reference repo in the notes.

[10:26] Jordan Lee: I'll flag two subtle engineering items we've seen: 1) KV cache format changes across quantized runtime builds — make sure you have migration paths if you keep long-lived caches, 2) RoPE scaling sometimes requires a small re-zeroing of rotary sin/cos buffers to avoid numerical drift at very long lengths.

[10:49] Dana Kim: About the earlier MoE pre-router idea — what is the overhead of that classifier? We'd add a small model in front — does that kill latencies?

[10:58] Priya Patel: Not if it's tiny. Distilled transformers or even a small linear classifier over bag-of-words features can be sub-ms. The key is to run it in the same process or low-latency sidecar to avoid RPC hops.

[11:12] Alex Rivera: Any tips for parameterizing the pre-router so it errs on the side of fewer top-2 calls?

[11:18] Priya Patel: Tune for recall of "needs multi-expert". You can bias the loss to avoid false positives. Also practical: sample the decisions in A/B mode for a few days to estimate real-world error rate before fully switching.

[11:32] Jordan Lee: Okay let's go through a quick live scenario from your logs, Dana?

[11:36] Dana Kim: Sure — we have a typical UI request: 512 tokens prompt, often ends up with 120 generated tokens; p90 latency target 220ms. Mostly single-user interactive. Roughly 60% of traffic is interactive; 40% is batch offline.

[11:51] Priya Patel: For that distribution we would: 1) keep interactive on a low-latency node pool with small batch caps and hot KV cache pinned, 2) for MoE routes use top-1 with selective top-2 via pre-router, 3) quantize candidate backup models (4-bit GPTQ Llama) for fallbacks. Should get you to 30–40% cost reduction without breaking p95 SLA.

[12:17] Alex Rivera: Can you share concrete numbers — like tokens/sec and GPU utilization targets?

[12:23] Marcus Huang: For a V100/A100 class node, with fused MoE kernels and pinned KV caches, you can expect ~1.8–2.2 tokens/ms for dense workloads; MoE effective tokens/sec depends on expert fan-out — a top-2 routing with 1.5 capacity factor often halves throughput unless you offset with extra experts. We'll include our benchmark table.

[12:46] Dana Kim: We also have regulatory constraints — logs must be retained for 365 days with auditability. Any performance impacts for detailed audit logging?

[12:56] Jordan Lee: Audit logging can be asynchronous — we stream request metadata and checksums to your audit collector. The cost is mostly storage/ingest, not inference latency, provided you don't synchronously block on audit writes.

[13:10] Alex Rivera: Any gotchas for mixing quantized fallback models in the same fleet? We worry about cache warming and format compatibility.

[13:18] Priya Patel: The main issues are: KV cache binary formats differ (floating point vs quantized approximations), and cold starts may need cache reclamation. Redwood's runtime can populate a canonical float KV cache and serve quantized kernels that read from a canonical buffer, or we maintain per-kernel caches and handle conversions asynchronously. Conversions add CPU cost but hide latency.

[13:42] Jordan Lee: Real quick, we touched on rope/positional — we'll paste a short script that does linear scale sweeps against your eval set. It takes about an hour to run on a single A100 for 2k eval examples.

[13:55] Dana Kim: That would be great. Also can you include an example of the pre-router model training script?

[14:02] Priya Patel: Yes — we'll share a notebook: small dataset, distillation recipe, and threshold tuning.

[14:10] Alex Rivera: Security — one last question: if we go Private (on-prem), what are the support SLAs?

[14:18] Jordan Lee: Enterprise private contracts typically include 24x7 support for critical incidents, a dedicated CSM, and a quarterly on-site review if required. SLA terms are negotiable. We'll list options in the security pack.

[14:33] Priya Sinha: Also, for SOC2 we need to know if debug traces can be redacted automatically.

[14:39] Marcus Huang: We have redaction hooks and masking filters at request ingest; they can be tuned per-tenant. We'll include the config examples.

[14:49] Alex Rivera: Great. Could we talk about one more micro-optimization — rope bucketed frequency?

[14:55] Priya Patel: Bucketized RoPE replaces the continuous angle with a small number of buckets and uses nearest-bucket mapping. It reduces drift at very large lengths, but introduces discretization errors. It can be good when you need deterministic behavior and small memory.

[15:11] Jordan Lee: We're approaching the last third of the call — any other blockers?

[15:17] Dana Kim: Just one: do you support custom operator kernels if we want to plug in our optimized scatter/gather?

[15:23] Marcus Huang: Yes — Redwood's dedicated and private runtime can accept custom kernels compiled into the runtime, with a verification step. We treat them as trusted artifacts for private deployments and have a code-signing step.

[15:37] Alex Rivera: Excellent. Let's recap next steps and who will own what.

[15:41] Jordan Lee: I'll summarize — Priya will run the routing sim and share a spreadsheet, Marcus will produce the network diagram and notes on HSM/KMS warm cache, I'll send security/compliance pack and pricing, Dana will export anonymized session stats, and Alex will propose two weeks for an on-prem pilot window.

[15:58] Dana Kim: Sounds good — I'll aim to have logs exported by next Tuesday.

[16:05] Priya Patel: I'll also include a short notebook for RoPE scaling and the pre-router distillation recipe.

[16:11] Alex Rivera: Thanks everyone, super helpful.

[16:14] Jordan Lee: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot and the deck + artifacts.

[16:20] (call ends)
